blocks.content: SQL DISTINCT covered removing duplicate rows from a result. SQL Aliases covers something different but genuinely practical, giving columns and tables clearer, temporary names, names that exist only for the duration of a single query, without changing anything about the actual underlying table structure.

This topic covers both column aliases and table aliases, why each one genuinely matters in real queries, and a specific case, the self join, where a table alias is not just convenient but genuinely required for the query to even work at all.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438200810-390026722.png
1. A Column Alias

A column alias renames a column just for the returned result, it does not change the actual column name in the underlying table at all, only how that specific query result labels it. This is genuinely useful for computed columns, ones built from an expression rather than a real, named column already existing in the table.
A column alias is written with the AS keyword, though many databases genuinely allow you to omit AS and simply place the alias directly after the expression, both forms work the same way in practice.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438200810-732409215.png
2. A Table Alias
A table alias renames a table, just for this one specific query, letting you refer to that table using a short, temporary name instead of its full, real name throughout the rest of the query.

A table alias becomes genuinely essential once a query joins multiple tables together, since referencing columns by their full table name repeatedly, orders.customer_id, customers.id, orders.order_date, gets verbose quickly, while short aliases keep the query genuinely readable.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438303978-162429657.png

3. A Worked Column Alias Example

A concrete query shows a column alias applied to a genuinely computed value with no real name of its own. An order_items table stores price and quantity separately, but a specific query needs their product.
SELECT price * quantity AS total_cost FROM order_items;
blocks.code: SELECT price * quantity AS total_cost FROM order_items;

codes.sql: SELECT price * quantity AS total_cost FROM order_items;

blocks.content: Without the alias, the returned column would genuinely have an unreadable default name, often something like the raw expression itself. With AS total_cost, the returned column is genuinely named total_cost, immediately meaningful to anyone reading the result.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438303980-148444181.png
4. A Worked Table Alias Example

A concrete query shows a table alias applied to shorten repeated references across a join. Two tables with genuinely long, real names, customers and orders, are aliased to short, single letter names for the rest of the query.
FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id
blocks.code: FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id

codes.sql: FROM customers AS c JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id

blocks.content: Once aliased, every later reference in the query can genuinely use c and o instead of typing customers and orders repeatedly, keeping longer queries with multiple joins genuinely readable rather than cluttered with long, repeated table names.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438303981-20661240.png

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.content: Trying to use a column alias inside the same query own WHERE clause. This genuinely does not work in most databases, since WHERE runs before the SELECT clause defines that alias, a detail tied closely to SQL execution order, covered as its own dedicated topic next.
5. Why Aliases Genuinely Help

A few real, practical reasons aliases matter. Computed columns get a genuinely real, meaningful name, rather than an unreadable default. Long table names shrink to short, genuinely readable prefixes, especially valuable once a query joins several tables together.

And self joins become possible at all, since joining a table to itself genuinely requires two distinct names to distinguish the two roles that same table is playing within one query, something only an alias can actually provide.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438303981-45439262.png

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: A self join, joining a table to itself to compare rows within that same table, genuinely requires aliasing the table twice, with two different names, since SQL cannot otherwise tell which reference means which role in the join.
6. Genuinely Common Mistakes

A few real patterns undermine alias usage. Using a column alias inside that same query own WHERE clause, which genuinely fails in most databases since WHERE executes before the alias is defined. Choosing alias names so short or so generic that they genuinely confuse the reader rather than clarify the query, a single unclear letter in a long, complex query can hurt readability rather than help it.
And forgetting that a self join genuinely requires two distinct aliases for the same table, without which SQL has no way to distinguish the two roles that table is actually playing.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438303981-872189739.png

A table alias renames a table just for one query, genuinely essential once a query joins multiple tables together.
AS is the standard keyword for both, though it is often optional and can be omitted in most databases.
A column alias generally cannot be used inside that same query own WHERE clause, due to real SQL execution order.
A self join genuinely requires two distinct aliases for the same table, since SQL needs a way to distinguish the two roles.
Aliases exist only for the duration of a single query, they never change the actual underlying table or column names.
